title: Gandhi and King
hook: a law student in London is handed his own family's book, in English
tomorrow: how does a Baptist pastor end up with a Hindu's method?

segments.voice: Yesterday in Gandhi and King, ahimsa: not-harming, and for Gandhi it had love inside it. Today, the book he kept going back to, and the strange place it opens.

Someone at a dinner party hands over a book your own family has kept for generations, in English, and asks what you make of it. You've never actually read it. That's where Gandhi is, as a young law student in London. Two brothers he's met there are reading the Bhagavad Gita in an English translation, and they ask him to read it with them. He's ashamed: he has never read it in Sanskrit, or in Gujarati, his own language. So he opens it. And the book begins with two armies lined up for war, and a god telling a frightened prince to stand up and fight.
screen: `A FAMILY BOOK, IN SOMEONE ELSE'S LANGUAGE.` → `A LAW STUDENT IN LONDON.` → `IT OPENS ON A BATTLEFIELD.`

segments.voice: So how does the man who wouldn't strike back end up calling this book his guide? In his autobiography, Gandhi says the Gita became his guide for daily conduct, a book he reached for again and again. His answer was a way of reading. Later he translated the Gita into Gujarati with his own notes, and named it Anasakti Yoga, the yoga of non-attachment. There he reads the battlefield of Kurukshetra as the human heart, where good and evil are always at war. Arjuna's real enemy is inside. Then he leans on a line from the second chapter: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. Do the work fully; let go of the result. For Gandhi, that line was the engine of nonviolent struggle. A satyagrahi could march, fast or go to jail without needing to see the win, because the work itself was the offering. Not every Hindu reads it his way. Other readers take the battle as a real war and a real duty, and the Gita has room for more than one reader. But Gandhi's reading hands over something steady. A setback isn't the end of the story, because the result was never the worker's to hold. The man of nonviolence found his steadiness in a war poem.
screen: `THE WAR IS INSIDE.` · `ANASAKTI: LET GO OF THE FRUIT.` · `THE WORK IS THE OFFERING.` · `MORE THAN ONE READER.` · then, large: `THE FRUIT WAS NEVER YOURS TO HOLD.`

segments.voice: If there's paper nearby, write down one task in front of you this week, the real one. Under it, leave a blank line where the result would go, and leave it blank. Breathe with the page in front of you: the work is written down, and the result stays open.
Gandhi and King: today, a war poem read as the war inside, and the work done without grabbing at its fruit.
Something to keep from Gandhi and King: the work is yours, and the fruit was never yours to hold. Until tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Gandhi's Gita: do the work, let go of the fruit. Saying it kindly is yours to do; her reaction isn't yours to hold.
